source_text: Harum uanitatum aput Romanos auctor et constitutor Sabinus ille rex fuit, qui maxime animos hominum rudes atque inperitos nouis superstitionibus implicauit: quod ut faceret aliqua cum auctoritate, simulauit cum dea Egeria nocturnos se habere congressus. erat spelunca quaedam peropaca in nemore Aricino, unde riuus perenni fonte manabat. huc se remotis arbitris inferre consueuerat, ut mentiri posset monitu deae coniugis ea sacra populo se tradere, quae acceptissima diis essent. uidelicet astutiam Minois uoluit imitari, qui se in antrum Iouis recondebat et ibi diu moratus leges tamquam sibi a Ioue traditas adferebat, ut homines ad parendum non modo imperio, sed etiam religione constringeret. nec difficile sane fuit persuadere pastoribus. itaque pontifices flamines Salios augures creauit, deos per familias discripsit: sic noui populi feroces animos mitigauit et ad studia pacis a rebus bellicis auocauit. sed cum alios falleret, se ipsum tamen non fefellit. nam post annos plurimos Cornelio et Baebio consulibus in agro scribae Petili sub Ianiculo arcae duae lapideae sunt repertae a fossoribus, quarum in altera corpus Numae fuit, in altera septem Latini libri de iure pontificio, item Graeci totidem de disciplina sapientiae scripti, quibus religiones non eas modo quas ipse instituerat, sed omnes praeterea dissoluit. qua re ad senatum delata decretum est, ut hi libri abolerentur. ita eos Quintus Petilius praetor urbanus in contione populi concremauit. insipienter id quidem: quid enim profuit libros esse combustos, cum hoc ipsum, quod sunt ideo combusti, quia religionibus derogabant, memoriae sit traditum? nemo ergo tunc in senatu non stultissimus: potuerunt enim et libri aboleri et tamen res in memoriam non exire. ita dum uolunt etiam posteris adprobare quanta pietate defenderint religiones, auctoritatem religionum ipsarum testando minuerunt. sed ut Pompilius aput Romanos institutor ineptarum religionum fuit, sic ante Pompilium Faunus in Latio, qui et Saturno auo nefaria sacra constituit et Picum patrem inter deos honorauit et sororem suam Fentam Faunam eandemque coniugem consecrauit; quam Gauius Bassus tradit Fatuam nominatam, quod mulieribus fata canere consuesset ut Faunus uiris. eandem Varro scribit tantae pudicitiae fuisse, ut nemo illam quoad uixerit praeter suum uirum mas uiderit nec nomen eius audierit. idcirco illi mulieres in operto sacrificant et Bonam Deam nominant. et Sextus Clodius in eo libro quem Graece scripsit, refert Fauni hanc uxorem fuisse; quae quia contra morem decusque regium clam uini ollam ebiberat et ebria facta erat, uirgis myrteis a uiro ad mortem usque caesam; postea uero cum eum facti sui paeniteret ac desiderium eius ferre non posset, diuinum illi honorem detulisse; idcirco in sacris eius obuolutam uini amphoram poni. reliquit ergo posteris Faunus quoque non parum erroris, quem tamen prudentes quique perspiciunt. nam Lucilius eorum stultitiam, qui simulacra deos putant esse, deridet his uersibus: terriculas Lamias, Fauni quas Pompiliique instituere Numae, tremit has, hic omnia ponit. ut pueri infantes credunt signa omnia aena uiuere et esse homines, sic isti omnia ficta uera putant, credunt signis cor inesse in aenis. pergula pictorum, ueri nihil, omnia ficta! poeta quidem stultos homines infantibus conparauit, at ego multo inprudentiores esse dico. illi enim simulacra homines putant esse, hi deos; illos aetas facit putare quod non est, hos stultitia; illi utique breui desinent falli, horum uanitas et durat. semper et crescit. sacra Liberi patris primus Orpheus induxit in Graecia primusque celebrauit in monte Boeotiae Thebis ubi Liber natus est proximo; qui cum frequenter citharae cantu personaret, Cithaeron appellatus est. ea sacra etiamnunc Orphica nominantur, in quibus ipse postea dilaceratus et carptas est; et fuit per eadem fere tempora quibus Faunus. sed quis aetate praecesserit dubitari potest, siquidem per eosdem annos Latinus Priamusque regnarunt, item patres eorum Faunus et Laomedon, quo regnante Orpheus cum Argonautis ad Iliensium litus accessit. procedamus igitur ulterius et quaeramus, quis omnino colendorum deorum primus auctor extiterit. Didymus m libris ἐξηγήσεως Πινδαριϰη̆ς ait Melissea Cretensium regem primum diis sacrificasse ac ritus nouos sacrorumque pompas introduxisse; huius duas fuisse filias, Amaltheam et Melissam, quae Iouem puerum caprino lacte ac melle nutrierint — unde poetica illa fabula originem sumpsit apes aduolasse atque os pueri melle complesse —; Melissam uero a patre primam sacerdotem Matri Magnae constitutam, unde adhuc eiusdem Matris antistites Melissae nuncupentur. Historia uero Sacra testatur ipsum Iouem postquam rerum potitus sit, in tantam uenisse insolentiam, ut ipse sibi fana in multis locis constituerit. nam cum terras circumiret, ut in quamque regionem uenerat, reges principesue populorum hospitio sibi et amicitia copulabat et cum a quoque digrederetur, iubebat sibi fanum creari hospitis sui nomine, quasi ut posset amicitiae ac foederis memoria conseruari. sic constituta sunt templa Ioui Ataburio, Ioui Labryandio: Ataburus enim et Labryandus hospites eius atque adiutores in bello fuerunt; item Ioui Laprio, Ioui Molioni, Ioui Casio et quae sunt in eundem modum. quod ille astutissime excogitauit, ut et sibi honorem diuinum et hospitibus suis perpetuum nomen adquireret cum religione coniunctum. gaudebant ergo illi et huic imperio eius libenter obsequebantur et nominis sui gratia ritus annuos et festa celebrabant. simile quiddam in Sicilia fecit Aeneas, cum conditae urbi Acestae hospitis nomen inposuit, ut eam postmodum laetus ac libens Acestes diligeret augeret ornaret. hoc modo religionem cultus sui per orbem terrae Iuppiter seminauit et exemplum ceteris ad imitandum dedit. siue igitur a Melisseo, sicut Didymus tradidit, colendorum deorum ritus effluxit siue ab ipso Ioue, ut Euhemerus, de tempore tamen constat quando dii coli coeperint. Melisseus quidem multum antecessit aetate, quippe qui educauerit Iouem pro nepote. et idcirco fieri potest ut uel ante uel adhuc puero Ioue deos colere instituerit id est alumni sui matrem (Opem) et auiam Tellurem, quae fuit Urani coniunx, patremque Saturnum et ipse hoc exemplo atque instituto Iouem ad tantam superbiam prouexerit, ut postea sibi diuinos honores auderet assumere.
pass_a_gloss: The author and founder of these vanities among the Romans was that King Sabinus, who most greatly entangled the rough and inexperienced minds of men with new superstitions: so that he might do this with some authority, he pretended that he had nocturnal meetings with the goddess Egeria. There was a certain very dark cave in the Aricinian forest, from which a stream flowed with a perpetual spring. He was accustomed to go there with the judges removed, so that he might be able to lie, with the warning of the goddess his wife, that he was handing over to the people those sacred rites which were most acceptable to the gods. Clearly he wanted to imitate the cunning of Minos, who hid himself in the cave of Jupiter and, having stayed there for a long time, brought forth laws as if they had been handed over to him by Jupiter, so that he might constrain men to obey not only his command but also his religion. And it was not very difficult to persuade shepherds. And so he created pontiffs, flamens, Salian priests, and augurs; he distributed the gods among families: thus he mitigated the fierce minds of the new people and turned them away from warlike things to the pursuits of peace. But while he was deceiving others, he did not deceive himself. For after many years, in the consulship of Cornelius and Baebius, on the land of the scribe Petilius under the Janiculum, two stone chests were found by diggers, in one of which was the body of Numa, in the other seven Latin books on pontifical law, and as many Greek books on the discipline of wisdom, written by which the religions not only those which he himself had instituted but also all the others were dissolved. Which thing having been brought to the senate, it was decreed that these books should be abolished. And so Quintus Petilius, the urban praetor, burned them in a public assembly of the people. Foolishly, indeed: for what did it profit that the books were burned, since this very thing, that they were burned because they derogated from religions, has been handed down to memory? Therefore no one then in the senate was not very foolish: for they were able to abolish the books and yet the thing not come out into memory. Thus, while they want to approve to posterity how greatly they defended the religions with piety, they diminished the authority of the religions themselves by testifying. But just as Pompilius was the founder of foolish religions among the Romans, so before Pompilius, Faunus was in Latium, who established nefarious sacred rites for his grandfather Saturn and honored his father Picus among the gods and consecrated his sister and wife Fenta Fauna; whom Gaius Bassus hands down as named Fata, because she was accustomed to sing fates to women, just as Faunus to men. Varro writes that she was of such great modesty that no man except her husband saw her or heard her name while she lived. Therefore the women sacrifice to her with covered heads and call her the Good Goddess. And Sextus Clodius in that book which he wrote in Greek reports that she was the wife of Faunus; who, because she had drunk a jar of wine secretly and had become drunk, was beaten to death with myrtle rods by her husband; afterwards, indeed, when he repented of his deed and was unable to bear the longing for her, he paid her divine honors; therefore in her sacred rites a jar of wine is placed covered. Therefore Faunus also left to posterity not a little error, which, however, all prudent men perceive. For Lucilius derides the foolishness of those who think that statues are gods in these verses: he trembles at the terriculas, the Lamias, which Faunus and Numa Pompilius established. Just as infant children believe that all bronze statues are living and are men, so these men think that all fictitious things are true, they believe that there is a heart in the bronze statues. The painting of the painters is nothing true, all is fictitious! The poet, indeed, compared foolish men to infant children, but I say that they are much more imprudent. For they think that statues are gods, those children think they are men; their age makes them think what is not, foolishness makes these men think; those children will certainly cease to be deceived soon, but the vanity of these men both endures and grows. The sacred rites of Father Liber were first introduced into Greece by Orpheus and first celebrated on Mount Cithaeron in Boeotian Thebes, where Liber was born; who, since he often resounded with the song of the cithara, was called Cithaeron. These sacred rites are even now called Orphic, in which he himself was later torn apart and torn to pieces; and he lived at almost the same time as Faunus. But who preceded the other in age can be doubted, since Latinus and Priam reigned in the same years, as did their fathers Faunus and Laomedon, during whose reign Orpheus came to the shore of the Ilians with the Argonauts. Let us proceed further, therefore, and seek who was the first author of the worship of the gods. Didymus in his books of the Explanation of Pindar says that Melisseus, the king of the Cretans, first sacrificed to the gods and introduced new rites and pomp of sacred rites; he had two daughters, Amalthea and Melissa, who nourished Jupiter as a child with goat's milk and honey — whence that poetic fable took its origin, that bees flew to him and filled the mouth of the child with honey —; Melissa, indeed, was established by her father as the first priestess of the Great Mother, whence the priests of the same Mother are even now called Melissae. The Sacred History, indeed, testifies that Jupiter himself, after he had become powerful, came to such great insolence that he himself established temples for himself in many places. For when he was traveling through the lands, so that in whatever region he came, he bound the kings and princes of the peoples to himself with hospitality and friendship, and when he departed from each one, he ordered a temple to be built for himself in the name of his host, as if the memory of the friendship and pact might be preserved. Thus the temples of Jupiter Ataburius, Jupiter Labrandius were established: for Ataburus and Labrandius were his hosts and helpers in war; similarly, the temple of Jupiter Laprius, Jupiter Molion, Jupiter Casius, and those which are in the same manner. Which thing he cleverly devised, so that he might acquire both divine honor for himself and perpetual name for his hosts, connected with religion. Therefore they rejoiced and willingly obeyed his command, and for the sake of his name they celebrated annual rites and festivals. Aeneas did something similar in Sicily, when he founded the city of Acesta and imposed the name of his host upon it, so that Acestes might later love and augment and adorn it with joy and willingness. In this way Jupiter sowed the seed of the worship of himself throughout the world and gave an example to others to imitate. Whether, therefore, the rites of the worship of the gods flowed from Melisseus, as Didymus handed down, or from Jupiter himself, as Euhemerus, it is certain, at any rate, from what time the gods began to be worshiped. Melisseus, indeed, preceded by a long time, since he educated Jupiter as if he were his grandson. And therefore it can be that he instituted the worship of the gods either before or while Jupiter was still a child, that is, his foster child's mother (Opis) and grandmother Tellus, who was the wife of Uranus, and his father Saturn, and that he himself, by this example and institution, provoked Jupiter to such great pride that afterwards he dared to assume divine honors for himself.

pass_b_english: Among the Romans the author and founder of these empty rites was King Sabinus. He tangled the rough, unlearned minds of men with new superstitions, and to give his deception some authority he pretended to hold nocturnal meetings with the goddess Egeria. A pitch‑dark cave lay in the Aricinian forest, fed by a never‑failing spring. Sabinus used to slip there after dismissing his attendants, so he could claim the goddess had told him to hand the people those sacred rites most acceptable to the gods. He was clearly copying the cunning of Minos, who hid himself in the cave of Jupiter, stayed there a long time, then produced laws as if delivered by Jupiter himself, thereby binding men to obedience not only by command but by religion. Persuading shepherds was no great feat. Accordingly he created pontiffs, flamens, Salii, and augurs; he assigned the gods to families. Thus he softened the fierce temper of the new people and turned them from war to the pursuits of peace. Yet while he fooled others, he did not fool himself. Many years later, in the consulship of Cornelius and Baebius, diggers on the scribe Petilius' land beneath the Janiculum uncovered two stone chests. One held the body of Numa; the other held seven Latin books on pontifical law and seven Greek books on the discipline of wisdom. These writings dissolved not only the rites Numa had instituted but all the rest as well. The senate decreed that the books be destroyed, and the urban praetor Quintus Petilius burned them in a public assembly. That was a foolish act: what good did burning them do, when the very fact that they were burned because they undermined religion has been preserved in memory? No one in that senate escaped utter folly: they could have abolished the books and still kept the matter from ever coming to light. In trying to prove to posterity how devoutly they defended religion, they testified against the authority of religion itself.

Just as Pompilius founded foolish religions at Rome, so before him Faunus did the same in Latium. He established impious rites for his grandfather Saturn, honored his father Picus as a god, and consecrated his sister and wife Fenta Fauna. Gaius Bassus calls her Fata because she sang fates to women as Faunus did to men. Varro writes that her modesty was such that no man but her husband ever saw her or heard her name while she lived. Therefore women sacrifice to her with covered heads and call her the Good Goddess. Sextus Clodius, in his Greek book, says she was Faunus' wife. She secretly drank a jar of wine, became drunk, and was beaten to death with myrtle rods by her husband. Later, when he repented and could not bear his longing for her, he paid her divine honors; hence a covered jar of wine is placed in her rites. Faunus too left posterity no small error, though every prudent man sees through it. Lucilius mocks the folly of those who think statues are gods, writing: "He trembles at the terriculae, the Lamiae, which Faunus and Numa Pompilius established." As infant children believe every bronze statue lives and is a man, so these men take all fictions for truth, believing a heart beats inside the bronze. A painter's canvas — nothing true, all fiction! The poet compared foolish men to infants, but I say they are far more imprudent. The children think statues are men; these men think statues are gods. Age deceives the children; folly deceives these men. The children will soon stop being deceived; the vanity of these men endures and grows.

Orpheus first introduced the sacred rites of Father Liber into Greece and first celebrated them on Mount Cithaeron in Boeotian Thebes, where Liber was born. Because he often sang to the cithara, the mountain was named Cithaeron. Those rites are still called Orphic; in them Orpheus himself was later torn limb from limb. He lived at nearly the same time as Faunus. Which of them was older is doubtful, since Latinus and Priam reigned in the same years, as did their fathers Faunus and Laomedon; during Laomedon's reign Orpheus reached the Ilian shore with the Argonauts. Let us go further, then, and ask who was the very first author of the worship of the gods. Didymus, in his books of the Explanation of Pindar, says that Melisseus, king of the Cretans, first sacrificed to the gods and introduced new rites and solemn processions. He had two daughters, Amalthea and Melissa, who fed the child Jupiter with goat's milk and honey — whence the poetic fable arose that bees swarmed and filled the boy's mouth with honey. Melissa was appointed by her father as the first priestess of the Great Mother; therefore the priests of that Mother are still called Melissae. The Sacred History testifies that Jupiter himself, after gaining power, sank into such insolence that he founded temples to himself in many places. As he traveled the lands, he bound the kings and princes of each region to himself by hospitality and friendship; when he departed, he ordered a temple built in his host's name, as if to preserve the memory of the friendship and pact. Thus arose the temples of Jupiter Ataburius, Jupiter Labrandius — Ataburus and Labrandius had been his hosts and allies in war — and likewise Jupiter Laprius, Jupiter Molion, Jupiter Casius, and others of the same sort. He devised this cleverly, so as to win divine honor for himself and give his hosts a perpetual name linked with religion. They rejoiced, obeyed his command willingly, and celebrated annual rites and festivals for the sake of his name. Aeneas did something similar in Sicily: he founded the city of Acesta and gave it his host's name, so that Acestes would afterwards love, enlarge, and adorn it with joy. In this way Jupiter sowed the worship of himself throughout the world and set an example for others to imitate. Whether the rites of worship flowed from Melisseus, as Didymus reports, or from Jupiter himself, as Euhemerus says, the time when gods began to be worshiped is at least certain. Melisseus preceded Jupiter by a great span, having reared him as a grandson. It is therefore possible that he instituted the worship of the gods either before or while Jupiter was still a boy — that is, the worship of his foster‑child's mother Opis, his grandmother Tellus (wife of Uranus), and his father Saturn — and that by this example and institution he drove Jupiter to such pride that he afterward dared to assume divine honors for himself.
